summary: Two linked goals for ages 6–7: automatic recall of addition and subtraction facts to 20 (so 7+8 and 15−8 come without calculating) and derivation of related facts to 100 by scaling and using known bonds — 6+4=10 → 60+40=100 by scaling the bond to tens, and 5+5=10 → 35+5=40 by using the ones bond inside a larger number. Recall is built from a secure make-ten strategy plus spaced, untimed retrieval rather than speed drills; derivation is built by treating tens as units so a known bond reappears at a larger scale.
misconceptions: Recall not automatic — still counting on fingers every time for 7+8
Failing to scale the bond: knowing 6+4=10 but giving 60+40=10 or 70 or 700
Treating addition and subtraction as unrelated, so 15−8 is re-counted despite knowing 7+8=15
Applying a derived pattern blindly (e.g. 35+5=40 but then 35+50=40)

activities.title: Same bond, bigger units: scaling 6+4 to 60+40
steps: Complete 6+4 on a ten-frame by sliding four counters in to fill all ten; confirm this is a known, secure bond making 10.
Switch the counters to tens: let each counter become a ten-rod (or restate each counter as 'one ten') so the same full frame now reads 100.
Say aloud what changed: 'six tens plus four tens is ten tens, which is 100' — the gesture and picture are identical, only the unit changed.
Repeat the tens-scaling with another known bond: 5+5=10 → 50+50=100 (five tens plus five tens is ten tens).
Separately, derive 35+5 by using the ones bond 5+5=10: 30 + (5+5) = 40, so here the 5 is added as five ones, not scaled to tens.
Deliberately contrast 35+5=40 with 35+50=85: in 35+50 you are adding five tens, not five ones, so the answers differ.
activities.insight: Deriving a decade fact like 60+40 is scaling a known bond, not memorising a new fact: six tens plus four tens is ten tens = 100. A different move is using a bond inside a larger number — 35+5 uses the ones bond 5+5=10 to give 40. Which unit you add (ones vs tens) decides the result, so 35+5=40 and 35+50=85 are different.

activities.title: Fact-family triangle: one trio, both operations
steps: Lay out the three numbers 7, 8 and 15 on a fact-family triangle (part–part–whole).
Cover one corner and read off the fact it reveals: cover 15 to get 7+8=15 and 8+7=15; cover 7 to get 15−8=7; cover 8 to get 15−7=8.
State explicitly: because 7+8=15, you already know 15−8 and 15−7 without re-counting.
Build a second family (e.g. 6, 9, 15, giving 6+9=15, 9+6=15, 15−6=9, 15−9=6) and name all its related facts the same way.
activities.insight: Addition and subtraction are the same relationship between three numbers; knowing one fact hands you the inverse, so 15−8 need not be re-counted once 7+8=15 is known.

activities.title: Spaced, untimed retrieval to build automatic recall
steps: Practise recalling facts to 20 in short, low-stakes sessions spread over days (e.g. 7+8, 15−8, 6+4, 9+4), rather than one long timed drill.
Mix in derive-a-fact prompts such as '6+4=10, so 60+40=?' and '5+5=10, so 35+5=?', choosing or writing the answer.
After each prompt, say which ones you just knew and which you had to work out.
Keep finger and make-ten strategy use welcome; the aim is that repeated facts need less effort each time, not beating a clock.
activities.insight: Automaticity grows from secure strategy plus spaced, untimed retrieval; a fact becomes 'known' when recalling it needs noticeably less effort on later encounters.

activities.title: Playful recall talk: 'how did you know that?'
steps: Trade quick spoken recall prompts back and forth with a partner or adult (flashcard-style), e.g. one asks 7+8, then 15−8, then 6+4.
For each answer, the asker follows up with 'how did you know that?' — did you just know it, make ten, or use the inverse?
Keep it low-stakes and untimed; celebrate strategy explanations as much as correct answers.
activities.insight: Verbalising recall and the reasoning behind it reinforces both the facts and the strategies (make-ten, inverse, scaling) that generate them.

checkQuestion: Rapid-fire, watching for hesitation and finger-counting: ask 7 + 8, then 15 − 8, then 6 + 4; then 'use 6 + 4 to tell me 60 + 40', then 'what's 35 + 5?'. Note which come instantly and which are counted out.
checkAnswer: 15, 7, 10, 100, 40. Fluent: 7+8 and 15−8 recalled (or via make-ten) without counting; 60+40 derived by scaling 6+4 (six tens + four tens = ten tens = 100); 35+5 derived from 5+5=10 → 40.
